steps: Check codes & permits
A building permit may be required. Install to NFPA 211 (U.S.) or CAN/CSA-B365-M93 (Canada) and local codes; mobile homes per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD).

Listed to ANSI/UL 1482 (U.S.) and CAN/ULC-S627 and CAN/ULC-S628 (Canada); safety tests by ITS, Intertek Testing Services. Anything the manual does not address defaults to NFPA 211 and local codes in the U.S., or CAN/CSA-B365-M and local codes in Canada; the local authority has final say.

Jøtul strongly recommends installation by a professional solid fuel technician, and a check with the homeowner's insurance company.
Unpack & inspect
Inspect for damage and contact the dealer if any is found; don't install a damaged stove. Leave the integral rear shroud on: it is the heat shield.

• Contents: miscellaneous hardware, single-wall 45° adaptor, double-wall starter collar P/N 227144.
  • There is no accessory stove heat shield. Do not remove the rear heat shield.
  • Tools: measuring tape, Phillips screwdriver, 10 mm and 13 mm open-end or socket wrenches, 4 mm hex key, work gloves, safety glasses.
Set the flue outlet
The cast iron collar exits at 45°. Single-wall: fit the supplied 45° adaptor (rear or top exit) with the two screws provided; double-wall: starter collar plus a 45° double-wall elbow (not provided).

• Single-wall: secure the 45° adaptor to the cast flue collar holes with the two screws provided. It must be used to keep the listed clearances.
  • Double-wall: secure the double-wall starter collar with the two screws provided, then attach a 45° double-wall elbow (not provided) with three sheet metal screws (not provided). Clearances by pipe brand: Table A, p. 15.
Connecting double-wall pipe to the single-wall adaptor violates safety compliance.
Run the chimney connector

6" black or stainless single-wall (24 gauge min.) or listed 6" double-wall; crimped end toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint. No more than two 90° elbows, 10 ft vertical single-wall, 3 ft horizontal with 1/4" rise per foot.
Qualify the chimney

Code-approved masonry with a tile or listed steel liner, or prefabricated Type HT (2100°F) to UL 103 / ULC S629; NFPA 211 Level 1 inspection before installation. Flue area no smaller than the flue collar's and no more than three times it (two times if outdoors).

• Masonry: fireclay liner 5/8" minimum thickness set in refractory mortar, at least 1/2" air space to the chimney wall; nominal 8" × 8" (no larger than 8" × 12"), or round with 6" to 8" inside diameter. Reline a larger chimney.
  • Brick or modular block 4" nominal minimum; stone at least 12". Airtight clean-out door at the base.
  • Prefab: tested and listed for solid fuel; keep the pipe maker's clearance (usually 2" minimum).
  • Existing chimney: Level I inspection by a professional sweep, fire official or code officer, with repairs done first; Level II when service conditions change or Level I is not enough.
  • No other appliance may vent into the same flue.
Check height & draft
At least 3 ft above the roof penetration and 2 ft above anything within 10 ft. Under 14 ft may not draft adequately; target .05 – .10 in. w.c. on a Magnahelic gauge, .07 ideal.

Inadequate draft shows as smoke spillage when loading or with the door open, back puffing and sluggish performance. Minimum height alone does not guarantee performance. Excessive height can over-draft, giving high stove temperatures and short burn times.
Wall pass-through (if any)

U.S. common method: clear combustibles 12" around the connector; a 6" connector needs a 31" × 31" opening filled with 12" of brick around a fireclay liner, 18" from combustible ceilings. Canada: clear 18" (43" × 43" for a 6" liner).

U.S. (NFPA 211)

Solid brick at least 3 inches thick (nominal 4"); liner ASTM C35 or equivalent with 5/8" minimum wall. Refractory mortar at the chimney junction; the pass-through liner must not extend past the inner surface of the chimney liner. Cut studs, add headers and a sill frame to carry the brick.

Canada (CAN/CSA-B365)

Pass-through at least 18" from combustible ceilings. The cleared space stays empty; sheet metal covers on both sides go on noncombustible spacers at least 1" from the wall (a single cover may be flush).

Listed prefabricated wall pass-through components may also be used.
Connect to the chimney

Masonry: slide the connector fully into the thimble to the liner's inner surface without protruding, and seal seams with refractory cement. Hearthmount: stove in front of a masonry fireplace, damper removed or fixed open, block-off plate sealed.

• Masonry chimney: a thimble sleeve slightly larger than the connector may be needed. Nothing may protrude into the flue liner or restrict draft.
  • Masonry fireplace hearthmount: 27" minimum opening on standard legs. Run the connector through the damper area into the chimney tile liner; seal a new sheet metal block-off plate around it at the damper frame (usually high-temp silicone). A full liner is recommended.
  • Prefab chimney: follow the pipe maker's instructions; usually a chimney adaptor on the bottom section, with the pipe fixed to it by two sheet metal screws.
Never install the stove inside a fireplace, or in any factory-built fireplace.
Mobile home requirements

Chimney components to UL 103 / CAN/ULC-S629, attached directly to the stove, 3 ft above the roof with a spark arrester; outside air connection and Floor Bracket Kit 157321 required. Keep all heat shields on, ground chimney, connector and stove; never in a sleeping room.

• Termination at least 2 ft above any part of the home within 10 ft; close clearance pipe; termination removable at or below 13.5 ft above ground without special tools.
  • Spark arrester: net free area at least four times the chimney outlet, height at least half the flue diameter; openings pass a 3/8" sphere but nothing larger than 1/2".
  • Outside air: direct connection required, no substitute method (Outside Air Kit #158265 on this page; p. 4 lists #157637). Duct termination no higher than the air inlet at the stove bottom.
  • Floor brackets go over the leveller screws at opposite front and rear corners, each with a 3/8" dia. lag screw (not supplied).
  • Chimney exiting below the roof at 7 ft or less above ground: guard up to 7 ft; a 3/4 in. rod must not pass, and a 1/2 inch rod inserted 4 inches must not touch the chimney.
  • Short legs are not approved for mobile homes. Maintain the structural integrity of floor, walls and ceiling/roof.
Do not install this appliance in a sleeping room.
Floor protection & clearances

Bottom heat shield stays on unless the stove sits on concrete poured on earth; size the non-combustible floor protector for U.S. or Canadian rules. Set wall clearances from the chart on p. 14, and Table A on p. 15 for double-wall pipe.

Use any continuous non-combustible material or a properly sized UL/ULC Type I or Type II hearth pad.

U.S.16 in. in front of and 8 in. beside the door opening; 30" × 40.5" rear exit · 30" × 43.25" top exit
Canada18" in front, 8 in. sides and rear; 39" × 48.5" rear exit · 39" × 47.75" top exit

Single-wall connector: 13" side / 14" rear / 10" corner to unprotected walls; 4" / 6" / 4" to protected walls. Alcoves take double-wall connector only.

panels.title: Weak draft · smoke spillage
items: Smoke spills when loading or with the door open → inadequate draft; chimneys under 14 ft may not draft enough
Back puffing, sluggish fire → poor draft
Short exterior masonry chimney → flue hard to keep warm; in very cold climates reline or extend it
Exhaust fan or clothes dryer running → low room pressure and flow reversal; outside air may help but isn't a guarantee

panels.title: Over-draft · over-firing
items: High stove temperatures, short burn times → excessive chimney height (over-strong draft)
Any part of the stove or chimney glows → over-firing; close the air control immediately
Door left partly open → over-firing, gas and flame drawn out of the stove
Warped plates, rust-colored cast iron, dusty-white paint → evidence of over-firing (not covered by warranty)

panels.title: Smoky, inefficient fire
items: Wet or unseasoned wood → heat spent driving out water; moisture condenses as creosote
No robust kindling fire → smoldering, inefficient burn
Smoldering, smoky fire → higher CO levels
Slow burning → tar vapors condense as creosote in the flue

panels.title: Glass & door seal
items: Sooty glass → low primary air setting weakens the air wash
Deposits left on the glass → etched, cloudy surface
Dollar bill pulls free easily → door seal too loose; remove a latch shim, then replace the gasket

start.title: Starting a fire
start.html:
Build the fire right on the floor of the firebox. Never use a grate or raise the fire up. Many people find this top-down method works best:

  1. Slide the air control all the way to the right (fully open).
  2. Lay two short quarter-split logs on the firebox floor, about 6 inches apart, running front to back.
  3. Lay kindling across them. Put one or two smaller split logs on top.
  4. Tuck newspaper between the two bottom logs, under the kindling. Light it and close the door.
  5. Add kindling and small logs as needed. Keep the air fully open until the fire is well established.
  6. Add more logs once the whole bed is burning. When a stove-top thermometer reads 400°F to 600°F (204°C – 316°C), set the air control for the heat and burn time you want.
A good burn looks like slow, rolling yellow-orange flames under the baffle at the top of the firebox, with little or no smoke from the chimney.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

The appendix (p. 24) also gives Jøtul's detailed cold-start method for the cleanest burn.

breakin.title: Break-in fires
breakin.html:
Your F 35 is steel with cast iron parts, so heat it up gradually over three fires. Put a magnetic stove-top thermometer on the cookplate, and start each fire with the air control fully open (all the way to the right).

  1. Fire 1: a small newspaper-and-kindling fire at the front. Add small pieces slowly, keep the stove at no more than 200°F (93°C), and burn at that low rate for about 1 hour. Let it cool to room temperature.
  2. Fire 2: up to 300°F (149°C) for 1 hour. Let it cool to room temperature.
  3. Fire 3: bring it up gradually to 400°F (204°C), then let it cool to room temperature. Break-in is done.
Running too hot? Slide the air control all the way to the left to shut off the air. The temperature may keep climbing until the wood burns down a bit. Never pull burning logs out to cool it. Once it's out and cool, carry on with the next fire.

Smoke and smell are normal at first

The high-temperature paint cures during the first few fires. It can smoke, smell and set off smoke alarms, and it fades with each fire. Open windows or doors for plenty of fresh air.

air.title: Using the air control
air.html:
One lever sets how hard the fire burns. Its handle is under the ash lip, below the door.

Slide rightMore air: hotter fire, faster burn
Slide leftLess air: lower heat, longer burn

Settings for best performance

High burnFully open
Medium burn1/2" open
Low burnFully closed

Open it fully when you start or rekindle a fire, or want more heat. More air also keeps the glass cleaner. Set a stove-top thermometer on the top, off to one side (Jøtul's magnetic one is accessory #5002). Once it reads 400°F to 600°F (204°C – 316°C), you can set the lever mid-range for an efficient burn.

Note: p. 2 gives the optimum stove-top range for the most efficient performance as 400°F – 700°F (205°C – 316°C); pp. 17 and 18 say to set the air control once the stove reaches 400°F – 600°F (204°C – 316°C).
The stove's minimum burn rate is set at the factory. Changing it is against federal regulations.

reload.title: Adding wood
reload.html:
Reload while the stove is still hot and has a bed of hot embers. Wear stove gloves.

  1. Slide the air control fully open (all the way right). Wait a few seconds for the draft to build, so smoke doesn't escape when you open the door.
  2. Open the door slightly and pause a moment to let the exhaust clear, then open it fully.
  3. Spread the coals and embers evenly with a poker or stove tool.
  4. Load the wood, usually smaller logs first. Keep logs at least one inch from the glass.
  5. Close the door and latch it tightly.
  6. Wait 5 – 10 minutes for the fire to pick back up, then set the air control for the heat and burn time you want. With an ember bed at least 2" thick, you may be able to set it right away.
The F 35 is rated for burns of up to 6 3/4 hours. The appendix (p. 25) walks through loading for high, medium and low fires.
Keep the door fully closed except while you refuel. Never push wood in with the door.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural, untreated wood only, cut to 16". The firebox is designed around that length. Longer pieces burn less cleanly, can keep the door from closing and can break the glass.

Dry wood burns best

  • Air-dried, seasoned hardwood burns most efficiently and cleanly. Wood dried for 6 to 14 months is ideal; wood dried more than 2 years burns too fast.
  • Seasoned logs have cracks (check marks) on the ends and feel lighter than fresh-cut ones.
  • Check with a moisture meter: aim for 12 – 20%. Wetter wood wastes its heat drying out and leaves creosote in the chimney.

Never burn

Coal, garbage, synthetic fuel or logs, unseasoned wood, anything containing plastic, rubber (including tires) or asbestos, manure or animal remains, lawn clippings or yard waste, waste petroleum products, asphalt products, paints, paint thinners or solvents, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, pressure-treated wood, salt-water driftwood or other materials previously saturated with salt water, paper products, cardboard, plywood or particle board. Burning any of these can release toxic fumes, cause smoke or make the stove ineffective. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust, wax or similar substances are fine for lighting.

ash.title: Removing the ashes
ash.html:
Scoop out the ashes whenever they build up close to the primary air port, the opening inside the firebox just under the door.

  1. Wear safety gloves.
  2. Put the ashes only in a metal container with a tight-sealing lid.
  3. Set the container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until you dispose of them.
  4. If you'll bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until every cinder has cooled completely.
Ashes can hide live embers. Only use a vacuum if it's made for ashes, and only once you're sure no embers are still live.

Regularly emptying all the soot and ash is part of the simple routine care that keeps the stove working well for years.

glass.title: Glass & door seal
glass.html:
Carbon and fly ash build up on the glass now and then. Clean them off before they sit too long, or the glass can etch and turn cloudy. Any creosote on the glass burns off in the next hot fire.

  1. Wait until the glass is completely cool.
  2. Use only a cleaner made for wood-stove glass, and follow its directions. No abrasives, and no ammonia-based glass cleaners.
  3. Rinse and dry the glass completely before you light the stove. Polish it with newspaper.

Burning with more air helps too: the air control also feeds a curtain of air that keeps the glass clean.

Open and close the door gently, and never use it to push wood in. Never burn with cracked or broken glass. Replace it only with Jøtul ceramic glass, part no. 224923.

Check the door seal

Close and latch the door on a dollar bill, then slowly pull it out. You should feel resistance. If it slides out easily, the seal is too loose. The latch is tightened by removing a shim; once that no longer works, the door gasket needs replacing. Both jobs are in the maintenance section.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
Slow fires make tar and other vapors that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. Built-up creosote can catch fire and burn extremely hot.

Check and clean

  • Inspect the chimney and connector pipe at the start of each heating season, then at least every other month while you're burning.
  • Clean the chimney whenever creosote and fly ash build up past 1/4 inch anywhere in the system. Your Jøtul dealer sells chimney brushes and can refer you to a professional chimney sweep.
Chimney fire? You'll often hear a roaring and crackling sound. Close the air control right away and make sure the door is shut tight. Call the fire department and get everyone out of the house. Don't try to put it out, and don't open the door to check: fresh air can make it flare up again.

After a chimney fire, don't use the stove until the connector and chimney have been cleaned and inspected for damage.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is extremely hot when it's burning, and touching it will burn skin. Keep children, clothing and furniture away. Use a child guard screen if small children are around.
  • Put smoke detectors in your living area and bedrooms. Test them regularly and change the batteries twice a year.
  • A carbon monoxide detector in the stove room is highly recommended. Place it, and any smoke detector in that room, as far from the stove as you can so it doesn't go off when you add wood.
  • Keep the door fully closed except when you add wood. Left partly open, the stove can over-fire and draw flame and smoke out into the room.
  • An exhaust fan or clothes dryer can lower the room's air pressure and pull smoke back through the stove. Talk to your Jøtul dealer if that happens.
Never over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney glows, you're over-firing. Close the air control immediately: a house fire or serious damage to the stove or chimney could result. Warped plates, rust-colored cast iron or paint turned dusty white are signs it has happened, and that damage isn't covered by the warranty.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Jøtul's limited warranty covers the original retail purchaser, from the date of purchase:

Baffle and air manifoldLifetime, parts only
Cast iron and steel parts5 years
Enamel finish (peeling, fading)2 years
Electrical parts1 year

Not covered

  • Wear parts: paint, gaskets, burn plates, firebricks, fire grates, ceramic insulation blankets and glass (glass is covered only against thermal breakage).
  • Damage from over-firing, misuse, rust (stove-top steamers can cause it), incorrect installation, or unauthorized changes or repairs.
  • Labor and travel costs, and damage in transit.
Keep your dated receipt. To claim, contact your nearest authorized Jøtul dealer. Jøtul must hear about a defect within 60 days of when it was found. Installation or service by anyone other than an authorized installer or service agency voids the warranty, and it can't be transferred. This is a summary; the full terms are in the manual.

specOutput.title: Heat output & fuel
specOutput.html:
Heat output range13,533 to 59,443 BTU/hr
Maker's website: Max Output (kW) 59.443.
Heating capacityUp to 1,200 sq. ft.
Maximum burn timeUp to 6 3/4 hours
Maker's website: Burn time up to 7h; its product data lists Burn time (h) 6.75.
Fuel16" logs (40 cm), front to back

Non-catalytic; listed to burn solid wood only. The output range comes from the EPA emissions tests; heating capacity varies with home design, climate, wood type and operation. Welded 3/16" steel plate with cast iron components.

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered; doing so is against federal regulations.

specEmissions.title: Emissions & efficiency
specEmissions.html:
Particulate1.2 g/hr (cord wood)
Carbon monoxide1.35 g/min
EPA efficiency · HHV68.5%
EPA efficiency · LHV73.67%

Meets the 2020 U.S. EPA emission limits for wood heaters manufactured after May 15, 2020. Particulate by EPA ALT-125 (cordwood), ASTM E2515 and ASTM E3053; efficiency and CO by CSA B415.1-10.

Section 5.1 (p. 16) states the HHV efficiency as 68.47%, and section 5.2 cites the CO test as CSA B414.1-10.

specFlue.title: Flue collar & chimney connector
specFlue.html:
Flue collarCast iron, exits at 45°
Connector6" single-wall or listed 6" double-wall
Single-wall pipeBlack or stainless steel, 24 gauge min.
ElbowsNo more than two 90°
Max vertical run (single-wall)10 ft
Max horizontal run3 ft, 1/4" rise per foot

No aluminum or galvanized pipe. Crimped (male) end toward the stove; three sheet metal screws per joint; 2 self-drilling screws from the hardware kit at the flue collar. Never slope horizontal pipe down toward the chimney. The connector may not pass through an attic, roof space, closet, concealed space, floor or ceiling, must stay accessible for cleaning, and is not a chimney. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to an air distribution duct.

Single-wall: use the supplied 45° adaptor (rear or top exit) to keep the listed clearances. Double-wall: use the double-wall starter collar (P/N 227144) and a 45° double-wall elbow (not provided). Double-wall pipe on the single-wall adaptor violates safety compliance.

specChimney.title: Chimney & draft
specChimney.html:
Above roof penetrationAt least 3 feet
Above roof or structure within 10 feetAt least 2 feet
Draft (Magnahelic gauge).05 – .10 in. w.c.; .07 ideal

Chimneys shorter than 14 feet may not provide adequate draft: smoke spillage when loading, back puffing, sluggish performance. Excessive height can over-draft: high stove temperatures and short burn times.

Approved chimneys (p. 6)

  • Code-approved masonry with a ceramic tile or listed steel flue liner.
  • Prefabricated Type HT (2100°F) to UL 103 or ULC S629; keep the pipe maker's clearance, usually 2" minimum.

Flue cross-section: not less than the flue collar's and not more than three times it; no more than two times for an outdoor chimney or one with a wall exposed below the roofline. Round fireclay liners 6" to 8" inside diameter; square nominal 8" × 8", no larger than 8" × 12". NFPA 211 Level 1 inspection before installation.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
From the clearance chart (Fig. 14, letters as printed). Protected walls: protection per NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365-M93.

Single-wall connector

Side (A / F)13" · 4" protected
Rear (B / G)14" · 6" protected
Corner (C / H)10" · 4" protected

Double-wall connector

Side (A / F)13" · 4" protected
Corner (C / M)9" · 4" protected
Rear (K / N)By pipe brand, Table A (p. 15)

Table A rear (backwall) clearance without wall protection, DW pipe at 6" · with wall protection, DW pipe at 2 ⅜":

ICC10 ⅛" · 6 ½"
Ventis11 ⅞" · 8 ¼"
Security10 ⅞" · 7 ¼"
Selkirk10 ⅜" · 6 ¾"

Table A also lists each brand's chimney centerline, hearth-extension front edge from the rear wall (U.S. / Canada), corner centerlines and 45° elbow part number. The chart's floor-protection columns give U.S. and Canadian values that are not interchangeable.

Double-wall pipe needs the double-wall 45° adaptor, never the supplied single-wall 45° adaptor.

Mantels & alcoves (p. 13)

Mantel and trim clearances are shown as a diagram (Fig. 13); they may be reduced by 50%, to a minimum of 18", with shielding built to NFPA 211. Alcove: double-wall connector only, wall and ceiling protection (if used) over the entire area, continuous non-combustible floor protection, minimum ceiling height 72" unprotected / 65" protected; short legs not approved.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
The bottom heat shield must stay on unless the stove is installed on concrete poured on earth. Otherwise use any continuous non-combustible material (metal, brick, stone, mineral fiber board) or a properly sized UL/ULC Type I or Type II hearth pad. Organic materials (plastics, wood, paper products) are combustible and not allowed.

U.S.

In front of door opening16 in.
Beside door opening8 in.
Under connector (rear / sides)2 in.
Minimum size30" × 40.5" rear exit · 30" × 43.25" top exit

Canada

In front of stove18"
Sides and rear8 in.
Under horizontal connector2 in.
Minimum size39" × 48.5" rear exit · 39" × 47.75" top exit

Drawn in Figs. 9, 9a, 10 and 10a (p. 12).

specHearth.title: Fireplace hearthmount
specHearth.html:
The F 35 can vent through a masonry fireplace, but the stove sits in front of the opening: never inside a fireplace, and never in any factory-built fireplace (p. 8).

Min. opening height · standard legs27"
Min. opening height · Short Leg Kit 15763623 1/8"
Note: p. 9 gives the minimum fireplace opening height on short legs as 23 1/8"; p. 2 says the short legs allow installation into a fireplace opening as low as 25 1/2".
  • Remove the damper plate or fix it securely open.
  • Run the connector from the flue exit through the damper area into the chimney tile liner; it extends at least into the first flue, and direct connection to the chimney cap is highly recommended (Fig. 7). A full liner is recommended.
  • Seal a new sheet metal block-off plate around the connector at the damper frame (usually high-temp silicone).
  • Flue area no more than three times the flue collar's (two times with any wall exposed below the roofline); reline if larger.
  • Short legs lower the stove by 3 1/4" and are approved only for code-approved masonry fireplace hearthmounts, not mobile homes or alcoves.

specAir.title: Outside air kit
specAir.html:
The kit's adaptor collar connects an exterior wall air inlet, through a duct, directly to the bottom of the fuel bed. A direct outside air connection is required in mobile homes. Elsewhere it can help where an exhaust fan or dryer depressurizes the room, though outside air will not guarantee chimney performance.

Note: pp. 2, 10 and 23 give the Outside Air Kit number as #158265; the safety notices on p. 4 give it as #157637.

Install

  1. Remove the four nuts and the bottom heat shield from the stove-bottom studs (10 mm), then the four remaining spacer nuts.
  2. Attach the outside air manifold directly to the stove bottom with four of those nuts.
  3. Remove the air inlet cut-out from the bottom heat shield with pliers.
  4. Attach the heat shield to the manifold with four sheet metal screws from the kit. If the heat shield won't be used, plug the manifold holes with those screws.

Buy locally: exterior air inlet cover, rodent screen, 4" aluminum duct and two 4" duct clamps. Install the exterior inlet lower than the stove bottom; in mobile homes the duct termination may not sit higher than the stove's air inlet.

review.notes: Single manual 130074_4 (page header 11/25; back cover reads 'October 2024'). Wood stove: no ignition system, no blower content (the TOC lists '5.5 Air Control / Blower Settings' but the section covers only the air control), no code table, no troubleshooting chart; the fault panels are built from the draft, over-firing, creosote and glass/door-seal descriptions on pp. 4, 6, 7, 16-20 and 31. p. 2 thermometer note: the degree signs are extracted as '0' ('4000 F - 7000 F (2050 C - 3160 C)'); read as 400°F - 700°F (205°C - 316°C) and flagged against pp. 17-18. Clearance chart p. 14: side/rear/corner values read from the lettered table text (single-wall A-C unprotected 13"/14"/10", F-H protected 4"/6"/4"; double-wall side 13"/4", corner C 9" / M 4", rear K/N per Table A); the unprotected/protected grouping is confirmed by Table A's K/N/C/M captions. The chart's floor-protection columns (D/E/I/J/L) were not transcribed because their headers are ambiguous in the extracted text; the Fig. 14 drawings were not transcribed. Mantel/trim clearances (Fig. 13, p. 13) and alcove dimensions (Figs. 11-12) exist only as diagram callouts; only the text rules are given. p. 12 also carries stray callouts (50 1/2" (128.3 cm), 2", 18", 8") that the text can't tie to a figure; worth checking against Figs. 10/10a. Table A: per-brand rear (backwall) clearances transcribed; centerline, hearth-extension, corner-centerline columns and 45° elbow part numbers summarized, not transcribed. Overall dimensions appear only as unlabeled callouts on Fig. 1 (p. 5), so none are listed; the catalog height/width/depth (28.75/20.25/30.25 in) match numbers on that figure but the mapping can't be confirmed from text. The manual gives no weight or firebox volume, so catalog weight_lb (385) and firebox_cu_ft (1.57) are unverified. Catalog feature text 'Burn time up to 7 hours' rounds the manual's 'Up to 6 3/4 hours' (p. 3); the catalog spec 6.75 matches. Catalog feature 'short legs drop the height to 25.5 in' can't be checked (manual: legs reduce height by 3 1/4"). HHV efficiency 68.5% (p. 3) vs 68.47% (p. 16) is rounding; both shown. CO test standard printed as CSA B415.1-10 (p. 3) and CSA B414.1-10 (p. 16). Manual cross-reference errors: p. 5 sends readers to figs. 22/24 on 'page 21' (they are on p. 23); p. 18 to Section 8.1 on 'page 22' (p. 24); fig. 35 and the parts list are cited as pp. 24 and 28-29 (actually pp. 26-27); p. 10 cites 'Appendix, Section 7.0' (that is Accessory Installation). The cover calls the unit a 'fireplace insert'; the parts list includes several 'F 45' descriptions. A French manual is offered at www.jotul.ca (not used).
